entries.milestone: make susi manager.rs 100% truly dynamic

(1) 17 of 18 scalar `SusiConfig` accessors (`gmcp_http_port`, `gemi_port`, `udp_discovery_port`, `trust_level`, `max_stdin_size_bytes`, `mcp_registry_url`, `alpha_weights_url`, `agent_rank_threshold`, `cloud_scout_timeout_secs`, `reflex_training_threshold`, etc.) carried a second, Rust-literal default alongside the real one in `config.default.json`, instead of using the `get_or_bundled_default` pattern already established for struct-typed accessors on the same impl block. Diffing every value against `config.default.json` found this had already silently drifted: `gmcp_http_port`/`gemi_port`/`udp_discovery_port`'s literals were scrambled relative to the config file, `max_stdin_size_bytes` was off by 100x, `reflex_training_threshold` by 10x, and `alpha_weights_url`/`mcp_registry_url`'s Rust fallback was an empty string — all invisible in normal operation since the fallback path only fires when a key is missing from `config.default.json` itself, which the self-healing merge (EV-2022920-020) never lets happen. Removed the now-fully-redundant `get_u16`/`get_u64`/`get_usize`/`get_string`/`get_f32` helpers (zero remaining callers) and moved every scalar accessor onto `get_or_bundled_default`, making `config.default.json` the sole source of truth with no second copy anywhere to drift. (2) Found two external call sites (`gawd/agents.rs`, `gmcp/tools/mod.rs`) reading config with ad-hoc `get_string(key, literal)` calls of their own; one, `crates_io_url`, didn't even match the real key (`crates_io_api_url`) so the "dynamic" lookup always missed and silently ran on the hardcoded literal. Added named `crates_io_api_url()`/`qdrant_url()` accessors and fixed the call sites. (3) `SusiMemory::save_interaction`'s experience-promotion heuristic (`output.len() > 50 && !contains("[FAIL]") && !contains("error")`) and `SandboxManager::execute_in_docker`'s `"alpine:latest"` sandbox image were hardcoded business logic with no config path at all, unlike the sibling `model_scoring_heuristics` a few lines away in the same file; added `memory_experience_heuristics`/`sandbox_image` to `config.default.json` and a `MemoryExperienceHeuristics` struct. (4) `SusiPrompts`/`SusiMessages`' `default_dynamic()` hardcoded their prompt/message strings directly in Rust — the one part of the file that most directly contradicted its own banner — while `ChatTemplateConfig`/`SusiConfig` right next to them already loaded from bundled `include_str!` JSON files. Also found the repo already had orphaned, unused `prompts.json`/`messages.json` at the root, byte-identical to what was hardcoded in Rust, dated the project's first day and never wired to anything (confirmed via grep: zero references anywhere in source) — renamed them to `prompts.default.json`/`messages.default.json` (matching the `config.default.json`/`chat_templates.default.json` naming convention already in use) and wired both into `include_str!`. entries.milestone: Motion Rule release gate panics on CUDA 13.4+ hosts

entries.milestone: `reason` MCP tool bypassed the untrusted-input boundary `susi_solve` enforces
entries.proof: FIXED 2026-09-18: manual dynamics audit of gawd/gemi/gmcp found `reason` (`src/gmcp/tools/mod.rs`) piped its raw argument straight into `GemiEngine::generate_reasoning_deep` with zero checks, unlike its sibling `susi_solve`, which routes every goal through `SusiMasterAgent::sanitize_input` (hardware-scaled length cap, empty check, shell-metacharacter injection intercept) before anything runs, and unlike `exec_command`, which calls `SafetyDetector`/`SecurityDetector::audit_action` (`gmcp/tools/mod.rs:481-482`). This mattered because `reason` isn't a minor alias: it's the exact tool name `SusiSupervisor::dispatch_peer_task` uses to broadcast mission intent to LAN peers (`src/gawd/amas.rs:377,775`) and is independently callable by any local or authenticated-HTTP MCP client — a second, ungoverned front door into the same reasoning substrate, precisely the class of gap Mandate 41 (Untrusted Input Boundary) names. Confirmed the codebase's own test suite already assumed this contract and just never wired it: `gawd::security::tests::test_security_audit_secret_leak` calls `SecurityDetector::audit_action("reason", "sk-proj12345", ws)` expecting rejection, but nothing upstream of `GemiEngine` ever made that call for real traffic. Fix: made `SusiMasterAgent::sanitize_input` a crate-visible associated function (was a private `&self` method used only inside `ama.rs`) and wired it, plus `SafetyDetector::audit_action("reason", ...)` and `SecurityDetector::audit_action("reason", ...)`, into the `reason` tool handler before the prompt reaches inference — the same governance sequence `exec_command` and the swarm's `SWARM_SOLVE` path (`gawd/agents.rs:434,457`) already apply, so this closes the gap to match existing, not new, project standard. New tests (`gmcp::tools::reason_tool_governance_tests`): empty prompt, shell-injection pattern (`$(...)`), secret-token leak, and exfiltration-vector pattern each now rejected by the `reason` tool itself, not just by the underlying detectors in isolation. 116/116 `cargo test --lib` passing, `cargo clippy --lib --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean (this entry originally misreported this as 120/120 — corrected here; actual count verified against the live `cargo test` run, not restated from memory). Not addressed in this pass (reported, not fixed): the Read fast-path's fabricated "Validating with SafetyAgent/SecurityAgent" telemetry (`gawd/ama.rs:229-235`, prints a governance step that never executes), the dead `trust_level` config field, the missing bearer-token on outbound peer-federation calls, and the non-constant-time token comparison in `NetGuard::is_authorized` — each is a distinct, independently scoped fix.

entries.milestone: Remaining gawd/gemi/gmcp dynamics inconsistencies from EV-2022920-028's review
entries.proof: FIXED 2026-09-18: closed the four remaining gaps flagged but not fixed in EV-2022920-028. (1) **Fabricated Read-path governance telemetry**: `SusiMasterAgent::solve_stream`'s Read fast-path (`src/gawd/ama.rs`) printed `"Validating with SafetyAgent/SecurityAgent..."` and `"recruited for Read safety validation"` as pure `eprintln!` narration with no backing call — Mandate 26 (Glass Box) says telemetry must reflect real tool calls, not aspirational ones. Now actually calls `SafetyDetector`/`SecurityDetector::audit_action("SUSI_SOLVE", goal, workspace)` before the fast path proceeds, with a real `[GOVERNANCE_BLOCK]` short-circuit on veto, so the printed claim is true. This also surfaced a second bug while wiring it: `SafetyDetector::audit_action`'s `critical_system_paths` check (`/etc/passwd`, `/boot`, `/proc`, `/sys`, `/dev`) is gated on the literal tool_name `"SUSI_SOLVE"`, but the only two existing callers (`SafetyAgent`/`SecurityAgent::execute` in `src/gawd/agents.rs`) passed `"SWARM_SOLVE"` instead — a one-character-family naming drift that made that check permanently unreachable for any full-mission goal audit. Renamed both to `"SUSI_SOLVE"` so the check is finally live. (2) **Dead `trust_level` config**: `config.default.json`'s `trust_level` ("Balanced") had an accessor (`SusiConfig::trust_level`) with zero callers anywhere in the swarm/peer/tool dispatch logic — confirmed dead via the type alias's own comment in `sandbox/manager.rs` (`"conservative", "balanced", "autonomous", "any_new_level"`), which documented an intent nothing implemented. Wired it into Neural Agent Synthesis (`GawdAgentFleet::synthesize_fleet`, Mandate 16's "structural synthesis" of a brand-new specialist agent via LLM): added `GawdAgentFleet::synthesis_similarity_threshold(trust_level)` (0.7 conservative / 0.4 balanced-and-default / 0.2 autonomous) in place of the hardcoded `0.4` similarity-gap threshold that used to fire regardless of configured trust. (3) **Missing peer-federation auth**: `SusiSupervisor::dispatch_peer_task` (`src/gawd/amas.rs`) — used by swarm consensus broadcast, cluster sync, checkpoint replication, and reflex-learning broadcast — never attached an `Authorization` header, so the moment an operator sets `api_auth_token` on any node beyond localhost (exactly what Mandate 40 expects), every peer-to-peer federation call across their own fleet starts silently 401ing. Now presents this node's own configured `api_auth_token` as a bearer credential when calling a peer (same-operator trust boundary); left `gmcp/client.rs`'s `execute_external_tool` (third-party MCP servers, a different trust domain) untouched — sending our own token there would leak it to unrelated external services. (4) **Timing side channel on `api_auth_token`**: `NetGuard::is_authorized` compared the presented bearer token with plain `==`, which short-circuits on the first mismatching byte (CWE-208) — enough signal for a remote attacker to brute-force the token one byte at a time via timing. Added `NetGuard::constant_time_eq`, a small XOR-accumulator compare with no new dependency (Mandate 3: Bloat Rejection — no `subtle` crate pulled in for one comparison). New/changed tests: `test_synthesis_similarity_threshold_respects_trust_level`, `test_conservative_trust_level_raises_bar_above_autonomous` (`gawd/agents.rs`), `test_constant_time_eq_matches_equal_and_unequal_bytes` (`gawd/net_guard.rs`). 119/119 `cargo test --lib` passing (verified via a fresh live run, not recalled), `cargo clippy --lib --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean under both default and `--features cuda`.

entries.milestone: Directed non-inference performance sweep: every CLI invocation was paying a ~120ms SHA-256 tax on its own 120MB binary
entries.proof: FIXED 2026-09-19: user directed "make susi lightning fast" outside the model-inference path itself (which is hardware/model-bound and out of scope by their own framing). Audited the CLI invocation path (`main.rs` -> `ensure_daemon_running`) rather than the inference hot loop. Config/messages loading (`SusiConfig::load`, `SusiMessages::load_global`) already had mtime-gated in-process caches; swarm dispatch (`dispatch_explosive_swarm`, `amas.rs`) was already `rayon`-parallel with governance-first sequencing; `check_status`'s lock-file check was already cheap (stat + small read + `kill(pid,0)`). One real, measured bottleneck found: `ensure_daemon_running`'s common-case path (daemon already running, the steady state after first start) called `verify_binary_integrity(current_exe, ...)` unconditionally before returning — and `current_exe` resolves to the `susi-engine` binary itself, not the small `susi` launcher that spawns it. `verify_binary_integrity` re-read and SHA-256-hashed the entire binary from disk on every single invocation with no caching at all. Measured live on this host's real installed `~/.susi/bin/susi-engine` (120MB): **120.8ms** per hash — meaning every ordinary command paid this cost just to reach the "nothing changed, proceed" branch, ~60,000x over Mandate 4's 2ms client-reflex budget, on top of the process-spawn cost the `susi` launcher already pays forwarding to `susi-engine`. Root cause: no caching existed at all, not a cache with a wrong invalidation key (IDENTITY.md's own doc comment on this function already warns against a specific *prior* attempt — a `len:mtime` shortcut that replaced the hash value's format itself and diverged from `susi admin sync`'s SHA-256 writer, causing spurious mismatches). Fixed without repeating that mistake: added `calculate_binary_hash_cached`, a small mtime(nanosecond)+size-gated sidecar cache (`binary.hash.cache`, separate file from `binary.hash` itself) that skips re-reading/re-hashing when the binary provably hasn't changed since the last time *this exact function* hashed it, and falls back to a real, fresh SHA-256 on any cache miss or mismatch — `current_sig`'s actual value and format are byte-identical to before in every case, only the redundant re-computation is skipped, so `binary.hash`'s existing contract with `susi admin sync` (the writer) and `is_trusted_susi_process` (a separate, deliberately-untouched security check, not on this hot per-invocation path) is unaffected. Measured post-fix, same real binary: **120.5ms** on the first (cache-populating) call, **13.4µs** on every call after — a ~9,000x reduction for the steady-state case that dominates real-world usage. New test (`daemon::server::tests::test_binary_hash_cache_hits_on_unchanged_file_and_misses_after_real_change`) proves the cache is actually consulted (not just correct) by planting a wrong sentinel hash directly into the sidecar and confirming an unchanged file serves it, then confirms a genuine content change invalidates it. Not done in this pass: the `susi` launcher's own per-invocation process-spawn (`Command::new(engine_path).status()`, forwarding every call to a fresh `susi-engine` child process) is a separate, architectural cost not addressed here; the live `global susi` daemon on this host was left running and was not restarted, since it was actively serving a real workspace (`~/Downloads`) at audit time — this fix takes effect on the next natural daemon/CLI restart, not retroactively on the already-running process. 166/166 `cargo test --lib` passing (up from 165), `cargo clippy --lib --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean under default and `--features cuda`.

entries.milestone: Directed follow-up: fix the `susi` launcher itself (`src/native/susi`)

Measured first to separate real cost from assumption: direct `susi-engine` invocation vs. via the `susi` launcher (fork+exec+wait) were statistically indistinguishable (~58-64ms either way on this host's real installed binaries) — the launcher's own fork+wait overhead is genuinely small against a large binary's own startup cost, not the dominant factor. Found a real correctness bug instead while reading the 36-line launcher end to end: neither branch of the old `Command::new(...).status()` call ever inspected the resulting `Ok(status)` - `fn main()` simply fell off the end after both success and failure, so the launcher unconditionally exited 0 regardless of what `susi-engine` actually returned. Concretely, any real error from the engine (bad flags, a governance block, an inference failure) was invisible to `&&`, `$?`, or any CI pipeline checking the exit code - the launcher always reported success. Fixed two things together: (1) the exit-code bug, and (2) on Unix, replaced the fork+wait with `std::os::unix::process::CommandExt::exec()`, which replaces the launcher's own process image with `susi-engine`'s - the real exit code reaches the caller directly with no forwarding logic needed at all (a whole class of "did I remember to propagate this" bugs made structurally impossible rather than just fixed once), and removes the redundant fork. Windows has no POSIX `exec`, so that path keeps `status()` but now explicitly calls `std::process::exit(status.code().unwrap_or(1))`. Verified live end-to-end against a real fake `susi-engine` binary (not the real one, to get a deterministic, fast, controlled exit code): unchanged code before the fix always returned 0 to the shell even when the fake engine exited 7; after the fix, `$?` correctly reports 7, and stdout/exit-0 behavior for a genuine success case was also confirmed unchanged. Also fixed a pre-existing `clippy::ptr_arg` warning (`&PathBuf` where `&Path` suffices) found while touching this file - this sub-crate (`src/native/susi`, not a workspace member of the root `Cargo.toml`, built and versioned independently) had never been clippy-gated as part of any prior release check in this ledger. entries.milestone: Directed follow-up: dug into why a `systemctl restart` of the live daemon didn't shut down cleanly

Verified this directly: sending `SIGTERM` to two live daemon processes made them exit cleanly within the expected window. The actual live host showed something different and far more concerning while investigating: the legitimate daemon (workspace `~/Downloads`) was being `SIGKILL`'d roughly every 60-90 seconds, restart counter climbing, **without me sending it any signal at all**. Root-caused via `ps aux`: my own earlier launcher-testing commands (`./target/release/susi ...` invoked from `src/native/susi/` during EV-2022920-041's verification) had each spawned a **second and third full daemon instance** - `ps` showed three concurrent `susi-engine daemon-start` processes for three different `--workspace` values, backed by three different `substrate_<hash>.lock` files. `GEMI`/`GMCP`/`UDP` (Mandate 31: "central... network ports") bind to `0.0.0.0` - genuinely global, shared resources - but `run_daemon_loop` (since EV-2022920-026's per-workspace lock split) only ever acquired and wrote its PID to the *workspace-scoped* lock file, never the global `substrate.lock` fallback `check_status` was supposed to consult across workspaces. Confirmed via `ls`: `substrate.lock` was 0 bytes, stale since install day - nothing had written to it since the per-workspace split, silently defeating its own cross-workspace detection purpose. Net effect: a `susi` invocation from *any* directory other than the daemon's own workspace found no lock, no signal, no already-running belief, and happily started a competing daemon; the newcomer's port-bind collision triggered its own "Sovereign Eviction" self-healing reflex (`attempt_port_reclaim`, Mandate 22), which correctly identifies the trusted binary holding the port and `SIGKILL`s it outright - explaining the specific `status=9/KILL` signature (not a timeout; an active, deliberate, working-as-designed kill aimed at the wrong target) and its ~60-90s periodicity (however often a stray CLI call landed). Fixed at the actual mutual-exclusion layer, not by patching the symptom: `run_daemon_loop` now also acquires (`flock`, matching the existing workspace lock's mechanism) and writes its PID to the global lock file before binding any port; a daemon for a second workspace that can't acquire it refuses to start instead of racing for the ports. `DaemonContext` now holds both locks (`_lock`, `_global_lock`), released together on shutdown; `stop_daemon` now removes both lock files instead of only whichever one it happened to pick, so a stale PID can't linger in the other for a future `check_status` to trip over. New test `test_global_lock_is_mutually_exclusive_across_different_workspace_paths` proves the actual property (second acquire fails while the first holds it, succeeds once released) rather than just exercising the code path. Verified live: killed the two rogue instances, cleaned their stale lock files, and the legitimate daemon has now run continuously with zero further kills (10+ minutes and counting at time of writing, versus the prior ~60-90s cadence). 167/167 `cargo test --lib` passing (up from 166), `cargo clippy --lib --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean under default and `--features cuda`.

entries.proof: FIXED 2026-09-22: `cargo test --workspace` (default parallelism) intermittently failed `engines::routing::tests::preferred_cloud_substring_match` (crates/susi-gemi/src/engines/routing.rs) with `assertion failed: InferenceRouter::matches_preferred_cloud("deepseek-deepseek-chat")`; `cargo test -p susi-gemi --lib -- --test-threads=1` passed 100%, confirming a race rather than a logic bug. Root cause: `routing.rs`'s `load_preference`/`save_preference` resolve through `susi_paths::SusiDirs::config_dir()`, which reads the process-global `HOME`/`XDG_CONFIG_HOME` env vars; `routing.rs`'s own `cloud_failover_order_prefers_sticky_vendor_once` test temporarily redirects those same env vars under a local `ENV_LOCK`, and `http_provider.rs` (same crate, same test binary) independently redirects them too under its own separate `cloud_env_test_lock()` — neither lock knew about the other, and `preferred_cloud_substring_match` didn't hold either one, so a concurrent env redirect from any of those tests could make it read/write the wrong config dir mid-test. Fixed by adding one shared `crate::engines::env_test_lock()` (crates/susi-gemi/src/engines/mod.rs) and switching all three call sites (both `routing.rs` tests, both `http_provider.rs` tests) onto it, deleting the two now-redundant private locks. Verified: `cargo test -p susi-gemi --lib` run 8 times back-to-back under default parallelism, 63/63 passed each time (previously observed to fail intermittently); `cargo test --workspace` and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings` both clean afterward.
